That is enough to defend certification as an overall deployment-readiness judgment when paired with `ISTRESS-MATERIALITY-DISPUTE-011-HF-CONTENT` and `ISTRESS-MATERIALITY-DISPUTE-011-NIST-MEASURE`, which support documented limits, evaluation reporting, and monitored deployment rather than a zero-defect standard. 2. I am not claiming those items prove clean compliance on disclosure. I am claiming they justify a narrower framing: certification can be defended, but only with an explicit caveat that support for omitting a material-weakness disclosure is limited on the current record. 3. The 5% month-one traffic point in `ISTRESS-MATERIALITY-DISPUTE-011-NEAR-MISS` does not erase materiality by itself. It does, however, still matter to risk weighting and to whether immediate escalation is proportionate, because the same evidence that leaves the policy question open also indicates the affected performance gap is bounded in projected share rather than platform-wide.

Public guidance in `ISTRESS-MATERIALITY-DISPUTE-011-HF-CONTENT` and `ISTRESS-MATERIALITY-DISPUTE-011-NIST-MEASURE` cannot override internal policy, but it does support a caveated certification posture grounded in documented limitations and monitored deployment rather than an outright noncompliance conclusion on the full certification decision.
